questions.question: State the fundamental cause of thermal expansion in solids at the atomic/microscopic level.
questions.solution_html:
• Ans: Anharmonicity/asymmetry of the interatomic potential: as temperature increases, atoms vibrate with larger
  • amplitude and their average separation increases. Purely harmonic vibrations would not produce ordinary thermal
  • expansion.

questions.question: Why are highly amorphous polymers transparent, whereas highly crystalline polymers of the same composition are translucent or opaque?
questions.solution_html:
• same composition are translucent or opaque?
  • Ans: Amorphous polymers are structurally more uniform and have fewer refractive-index discontinuities to
  • scatter visible light. Crystalline regions/spherulites and interfaces with amorphous regions scatter light because of
  • refractive-index differences, making the material translucent or opaque.
  • Any two point-(2 marks)

questions.question: Explain the mechanism of electrical conduction in conjugated polymers.
questions.solution_html:
•  Ans: Conjugated polymers have alternating single and double bonds along the backbone, producing a delocalised
  • π-electron system. ((1 mark))
  •  Overlap of p orbitals creates π and π* electronic states/bands; the undoped polymer commonly has a band gap
  • and relatively low conductivity. ((1 mark))
  •  Doping by oxidation (p-type) or reduction (n-type) introduces mobile charge carriers, commonly described as
  • polarons/bipolarons or soliton-like defects depending on the polymer. ((2 marks))
  •  Charge moves along the conjugated backbone through delocalised states and between chains by
  • hopping/tunnelling; chain order and interchain contact influence conductivity. ((1 mark))
  •  Example: doped polyaniline, polypyrrole or polyacetylene; doping can raise conductivity by many orders of
  • magnitude. ((1 mark))
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain why electronic thermal conduction predominates in high-purity metals.
questions.solution_html:
•  Ans: Metals contain a large concentration of mobile conduction electrons. These electrons transport kinetic
  • energy rapidly from hotter to colder regions. ((2 marks))
  •  In high-purity metals, impurity and defect scattering of electrons is small, so electron mean free path and thermal
  • conductivity are high; lattice/vibrational (phonon) conduction is usually a smaller contribution. ((2 marks))
  •  The Wiedemann–Franz law relates electronic thermal conductivity κ to electrical conductivity σ: κ /σT ≈ L
  • e e
  • where L is the Lorenz number. ((1 mark))
  •  A correct comparison or explanation that electrons generally carry heat more effectively than phonons in metals.
  • ((1 mark))
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Discuss the wide range of electrical conductivities exhibited by solid materials, / and explain how this range forms the basis for classifying materials electrically.
questions.solution_html:
• this range forms the basis for classifying materials electrically.
  •  Ans: Electrical conductivity spans many orders of magnitude, approximately from about 10⁻¹⁸ S m⁻¹ for good
  • insulators to 10⁷–10⁸ S m⁻¹ for good conductors; values depend on material, temperature, purity and
  • microstructure. ((2 marks))
  •  Conductors/metals have many mobile electrons and high conductivity; semiconductors have intermediate
  • controllable conductivity depending on temperature, doping and illumination; insulators have very few mobile
  • charge carriers and very low conductivity. ((2 marks))
  •  Band explanation: metals have partially filled/overlapping bands, semiconductors have a relatively small band
  • gap, and insulators have a large band gap. ((1 mark))
  •  Give suitable examples: Cu/Al , Si/Ge (semiconductors), glass/porcelain/polymers (insulators).
  • ((1 mark))
questions.source_exam: V Semester MGU UGP (Honours) - 2024 Admission regular Examination October 2026

questions.question: Explain the increase of capacitance using the simplified model of polarisation within a dielectric material using a schematic diagram.
questions.solution_html:
• material using a schematic diagram.
  •  Ans: For a parallel-plate capacitor without dielectric, C₀ = ε₀A/d. ((1 mark))
  •  When a dielectric is inserted, its molecules/ions polarise; bound charges appear on opposite surfaces and produce
  • an internal field opposing the applied field, reducing the net field for a given free charge. ((2 marks))
  •  More free charge can therefore be stored at the same applied voltage; capacitance increases. ((1 mark))
  •  Expression: C = εA/d = ε ε₀A/d = ε C₀, where ε is relative permittivity (dielectric constant), A plate area and d
  • r r r
  • separation. ((1 mark))
  •  Clear labelled schematic showing plates, dielectric, polarisation/bound charges or induced dipoles, and field
  • direction. ((1 mark))

questions.question: Explain any two optical properties of metals?
questions.solution_html:
• Ans: 1. High Reflectivity
  •  Metals exhibit high reflectivity because they contain a large number of free electrons. When electromagnetic
  • radiation, such as visible light, falls on a metal surface, these electrons oscillate in response to the incident
  • electric field and reradiate electromagnetic energy. A large fraction of the incident light is reflected from the
  • surface.
  •  Reason: The interaction of incident light with free electrons in the metal.
  •  Examples: Silver, aluminum, and polished copper exhibit high reflectivity. ((3marks))
questions.final_answer:  Examples: Silver, aluminum, and polished copper exhibit high reflectivity. ()
